item.title: The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership
item.description:
The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership Expert comment thilton.drupal 16 November 2026

The UK–EU Summit is an opportunity to secure a new partnership suitable for an increasingly hostile global economy. It should start with an information-sharing arrangement about high-risk investments, including from China.

The second UK–EU ‘reset’ summit takes place on 20 November, after a six-month delay to give prime minister Andy Burnham’s new government time to settle in and set its priorities. 

It is expected to deliver on the deals kickstarted by the Starmer government, most of which focus on reducing barriers to trade and mobility. These include a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement that removes most checks on trade in animals, plants, and their products, as well as a youth experience scheme and the linking of the UK and EU emissions trading systems. Completing these agreements is important for growth – the UK government estimates the SPS deal could eventually be worth £5.1 billion a year – and for building trust with the EU after years of political setbacks.

But the Burnham government will likely also want a more strategic partnership with the EU on security, defence and geopolitics. Central to this should be the goal of economic security, which has become a key priority for governments around the world. Economic security revolves around protecting sensitive national assets from hostile interference or exploitation, withstanding coercion and supply shocks, and building the strategic capabilities needed to stay competitive.

Beyond ‘Made in Europe’

Much of the reporting on this topic has focused on whether UK firms will be covered by the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiatives. These measures – the most significant of which are in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act – favour European-made products in public procurement and subsidy schemes, with the aim of rebuilding the EU’s industrial base and reducing its strategic dependencies. The concern is that, unless UK-made goods are treated the same as European-made ones, these initiatives risk shutting UK firms out of European supply chains.

Related work

Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose 

For now, the decision over ‘Made in Europe’ appears to have been kicked into next year. But ‘Made in Europe’ is only one part of the picture, albeit a critical one. Since Brexit, the global economy has become far more adversarial. The US is more willing to use tariffs as bargaining chips, while China is restricting exports of critical inputs such as rare earths to advance its geopolitical goals. 

In a forthcoming paper, we argue that middle powers such as the UK need to work together to manage these pressures. Partners like Australia, Canada, Japan and South Korea will be critical. But the EU is the UK’s most consequential economic security partner, due to its proximity, integrated supply chains and shared security interests. The UK’s approach to the upcoming summit should therefore put economic security cooperation as a crucial pillar of the reset in UK–EU relations.

Economic security partnership

The UK and the EU share challenges ranging from coercion and Chinese overcapacity to an unpredictable US. They also have shared dependencies in critical minerals, energy and some advanced technologies. 

A new UK–EU economic security partnership would give both sides a regular, structured mechanism to share information and coordinate on these risks. 

This partnership could build on existing structures. These could include the Partnership Council set up in 2021 under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the 2025 Security and Defence Partnership, and the annual UK–EU summits. The partnership would also involve designated channels being established across each government to coordinate information-sharing and policy objectives as part of its structure. 

As part of this partnership, the EU and the UK should initiate an annual ministerial dialogue on economic security, supported by official-level working groups. This would compare assessments of geo-economic risks, including from China, and discuss approaches to coercion, industrial policy and overcapacity. It should also consider ways to jointly engage other like-minded partners on trade norms and to address geo-economic shocks, such as the energy price crisis that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

From the outset, the partnership should also include a commitment to consult on how to respond if either side faces retaliation for measures taken together. This could apply if the UK were to align with EU tariffs or investment conditions on Chinese goods or capital, for example as part of securing ‘Made in Europe’ treatment. In this scenario, the UK should act within an agreed process for managing any consequences. That would give both sides a framework within which to negotiate how to align their economic security.

Start with protective tools

Aligning tariffs and industrial policy is politically and economically challenging. This is partly because the UK and the EU compete in certain industrial sectors and for investment. It’s also because the UK sits outside the trading bloc and cannot currently benefit from the EU’s single market or the Anti-Coercion Instrument (nicknamed the ‘trade bazooka’), its new trade tool aimed at deterring and responding to economic coercion. 

Rather than initially seeking this alignment, the partnership should therefore instead begin by strengthening cooperation to address the risks posed by hostile actors acquiring or accessing sensitive assets. These include data, technology and intellectual property.

Related work

China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one

At present, the UK and the EU share too little information on investment risks, research security and vulnerabilities in critical supply chains. Closer cooperation in these areas carries lower political and economic costs than aligning on tariffs. And it plays to the UK’s strengths. 

The UK’s National Security and Investment Act (NSIA) is one of the more developed screening regimes in Europe, while the EU only recently made it mandatory for all member states to screen investments for national security risks. A practical first step would be an information-sharing arrangement between the UK’s Investment Security Unit and EU member states’ screening authorities. This would also help address concerns on both sides about high-risk investments, including those from China. 

Over time, this would make it easier to share sensitive technology, capital and research. It would help build the trust needed for harder decisions on industrial policy and trade defence. 

A more ambitious agenda

Once that trust is established, the partnership should pursue a more ambitious agenda. First, this should build on the information-sharing set out above to establish a joint early warning arrangement for supply-chain disruption as soon as possible, modelled on the aims of the US-Japan-South Korea system, connecting the UK’s Supply Chain Centre with the EU’s monitoring of critical goods. 

Over the next two years, it should also include a channel for coordinating responses to coercion, including how the UK’s emerging anti-coercion framework could work alongside the EU’s Anti-Coercion Instrument. And it should foster strategic industrial collaboration over the long term, including pooling resources and talent. 

However, while political will is growing on both sides, cooperation on economic security still faces challenges. The EU is wary of extending subsidy and procurement benefits without commitments that ensure reciprocal access to UK schemes and alignment on tariffs and investment conditions towards China. For its part, the UK will resist overt rule-taking or limits on its freedom to set its own trade policy. 

The best way to begin addressing some of these challenges is to start with information-sharing, which asks less of either side than full alignment. It would start to answer EU concerns about Chinese investment and build the trust both sides need for harder decisions later. 

The effort is worth it. Despite Brexit, the UK’s long-term economic future ultimately remains closely tied to Europe’s. 

This is particularly true when it comes to shared economic security. A forward-looking UK–EU economic security partnership would help protect both economies from coercion and supply shocks, strengthening the industries that both will depend on while navigating an increasingly hostile global economy.

item.title: Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice

It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet his final downfall remains far from certain.

As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump, his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palestinians in the West Bank and in hungry, flooded Gaza, and the bombed and battered people of Iran, have good reason to be fearful.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Pakistan’s hopes of lifting their maiden SAFF Championship title ended in heartbreak on Tuesday as defending champions India came from behind to secure a 2-1 victory in the final at the National Stadium, extending their record to 10 titles and completing an unprecedented hat-trick of consecutive triumphs.

The Shaheens produced an impressive first-half display and looked on course for a historic victory after taking the lead through Alamgir Ghazi in stoppage time.

However, the dismissal of defender Junaid Shah early in the second half proved a turning point, allowing India to seize control and score twice to retain their crown.

Pakistan, appearing in their first-ever SAFF Championship final, began confidently and enjoyed the better of the opening exchanges, putting India’s reshuffled side under sustained pressure.

The Green Shirts threatened repeatedly down the flanks, with the combination of Abdul Samad Arshad and Haris Zeb causing problems for the Indian defence.

India, meanwhile, struggled to establish attacking rhythm, although they came close to scoring around the 35th minute when Pakistan goalkeeper Yousuf Butt produced an important save to deny a dangerous effort.

Just when the first half appeared destined to end goalless, Pakistan broke the deadlock in spectacular fashion.

Junaid Shah delivered a cross from the left during first-half stoppage time which took a deflection off an Indian defender before falling to Alamgir inside the penalty area.

The midfielder made no mistake, curling a superb right-footed effort into the far corner to send Pakistan into the interval with a deserved 1-0 advantage.

India returned after the break with greater urgency and immediately began pushing forward in search of an equaliser. Yousuf was called into action in the 51st minute, denying PV Vishnu after the Indian midfielder made his way through the Pakistan defence.

The contest, however, took a dramatic turn in the 60th minute when a Video Assistant Referee (VAR) review resulted in Junaid being shown a straight red card for a reckless challenge on Brison Fernandes.

Reduced to 10 men, Pakistan struggled to contain the defending champions, who wasted little time capitalising on their numerical advantage.

India restored parity almost immediately when a free-kick delivery from Lhungdim Khaiminthang caused problems inside the penalty area. Macarton Nickson got a slight touch before Suhail Ahmad Bhat side-footed the ball into the net to make it 1-1.

The equaliser shifted the momentum firmly in India’s favour as Pakistan were forced to retreat and defend deep. Butt kept his side in contention with another important intervention in the 67th minute, turning away an effort from Vishnu.

Pakistan coach Nolberto Solano responded with substitutions, withdrawing Alamgir as he attempted to reorganise his depleted side. However, India continued to dominate possession and press for a decisive goal.

Their persistence finally paid off in the 88th minute when a corner created confusion inside the Pakistan penalty area. Sandip Mandi found himself unmarked and headed past Yousuf to put India ahead for the first time in the match.

Pakistan threw players forward during the closing stages in a desperate attempt to force an equaliser, but India held firm through five minutes of added time to secure victory.

The defeat was particularly painful for Pakistan, who had reached the final after defeating hosts Bangladesh 1-0 in the semi-final, courtesy of Abdul Samad Arshad’s late winner.

Despite falling short of the title, the Shaheens’ run to their first-ever final marked a significant milestone for the national side.

For India, meanwhile, the victory reinforced their regional dominance, taking their SAFF Championship tally to 10 titles and making them the first team to win three successive editions of the tournament.

item.title: Bangladesh garment workers, police clash in fresh wage protest
item.description:
Bangladeshi police fired tear gas and stun grenades on Tuesday in clashes with thousands of garment workers who were protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.

Protesters hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between capital Dhaka and key financial district Mymensingh as demonstrations demanding higher wages turned violent.

The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for major international brands including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.

But growing worker unrest over wages that began in October has threatened to disrupt the industry that generates $38 billion in revenues annually and employs more than four million people.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) — a 140-per cent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.

Some 500 factories out of 4,500 are shut, sources told AFP, something that is further stoking unrest among workers.

A “no work, no pay” provision of the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” said Khanom, 24, who gave only one name.

Tensions were also running high in the other garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on the outskirts of Dhaka.

The wage board, comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.

‘Monitoring cell’

The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January.

“We want to return to our machines,” said Rakib, 28, another garment worker.

“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.

Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.

In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.

A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a source in BGMEA told AFP.

The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.

In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.

“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.

The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

The country’s garment industry makes clothes for some of the world’s best-known brands but the sector has been marred by longstanding disputes over wages, working conditions and labour rights.

The United States is its biggest individual market, while the European Union is its largest trading bloc.

The latest disruption comes during the run-up to Christmas, the busiest export period for Bangladesh’s garment industry.

item.title: Shane Deitz appointed Pakistan women’s team head coach
item.description:
The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Tuesday appointed Australian Shane Deitz as head coach of the national women’s cricket team, with the 51-year-old set to take charge ahead of the forthcoming bilateral series against West Indies.

Deitz will join the Pakistan squad in the Caribbean for his first assignment, replacing Wahab Riaz, who had been serving as mentor and head coach following the departure of former Test batter Mohammad Wasim after last year’s ICC Women’s World Cup.

He becomes the third foreign coach to take charge of the Pakistan women’s team, following New Zealand’s Mark Coles, who had two stints in the role, and Bermuda’s David Hemp. His appointment also marks a return to a foreign coaching option after a period of local coaches.

In a statement issued by the PCB, Deitz said he was honoured to take up the position, recalling his memories of supporting Pakistan during the 1992 World Cup final against England.

“I am very honoured to become the head coach of the Pakistan women’s team. Pakistan cricket has a tremendous history and I remember fondly cheering them on as a youngster in Australia at the 1992 World Cup final against England, which was a great achievement for Pakistan cricket,” he said.

Deitz said the team’s long-term objective would be to give supporters something to cheer about when Pakistan hosts the T20 World Cup in 2028. He acknowledged that considerable work lay ahead for the players and coaching staff to produce world-class performances.

Playing and coaching background

Hailing from Bankstown, New South Wales, Deitz was a left-handed top-order batter who also occasionally kept wickets.

After representing New South Wales at junior level, he moved to South Australia, where he played 66 first-class matches for the Redbacks between 1998-99 and 2007-08.

Following his retirement, Deitz moved into coaching, initially serving as a high-performance coach with Cricket Wellington in New Zealand from 2008 to 2013.

He subsequently coached Bangladesh’s women’s team in 2013-14 before taking up various roles with Vanuatu Cricket, including national coach and chief executive.

From around 2020 to 2023, he coached the Netherlands women’s team, helping the side regain ODI status.

In July 2023, Deitz was appointed head coach of the West Indies women’s team. Under his guidance, the Caribbean side reached the semi-finals of consecutive ICC Women’s T20 World Cups in 2024 and 2026.

His contract with Cricket West Indies expired at the end of October 2026, with both parties mutually agreeing to part ways.

Frequent changes in coaching set-up

The Pakistan women’s team has witnessed considerable instability in its coaching set-up in recent years, with Deitz becoming the sixth person to take charge in the past three and a half years.

Coles, the first foreign coach of the team, served from 2017 to 2019 before briefly returning in 2023. However, he resigned during his second stint for personal reasons.

Hemp succeeded Coles and remained in the role from 2020 until around 2022.

Subsequent appointments included local coaches and interim arrangements, with Wasim taking charge ahead of the 2024 Asia Cup before his departure following the World Cup.

Wahab subsequently oversaw the team as mentor and head coach during a mixed period that included a solitary victory at the T20 World Cup, a semi-final appearance at the Asia Cup and a bronze medal at the Asian Games, alongside a number of series defeats.

Pakistan are currently featuring in the ICC Emerging Nations Trophy in the United Arab Emirates.

item.title: Shama: India’s reported conditions for Hasina’s return have no legal basis
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam has dismissed reports that India has set conditions for the return of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, saying the reported demands have no basis in Bangladesh's laws.
Responding to reports that India had sought to ensure Hasina's right to appeal and restart her trial before agreeing to her return, Shama said Bangladesh had received no such proposal.
“No, not at all. We have had no such conversations with them on this matter,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, referring to reports published by BBC Bangla.
She said Bangladesh expects Hasina, who has been sentenced to death for crimes against humanity, to be brought back from India under the existing extradition treaty.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has written to India multiple times under the extradition treaty,” she said, adding that the Ministries of Law and Home Affairs are examining the legal and technical aspects of the matter.
Shama said the government believes Hasina, like any other accused person, should be returned under the treaty to serve her sentence.
She also questioned whether Hasina's Bangladeshi citizenship alone would guarantee her the right to obtain a passport, saying the relevant laws do not require the government to issue passports to convicted criminals or individuals facing serious cases.
On bilateral relations, Shama said Bangladesh-India ties extend far beyond the issue of Hasina, emphasizing the longstanding relationship between the 2 neighboring countries and the importance of addressing bilateral matters through diplomacy.
“Bangladesh-India relations are a much bigger deal than Sheikh Hasina,” she said, urging against giving the issue more importance than necessary.
“We have issues. We will deal with the issues through diplomacy,” she said.
However, Shama said the government could not ignore Hasina's activities in India if they were aimed at destabilizing Bangladesh.
Regarding the Bangladesh-India Consular Dialogue, originally scheduled for November 17-18, Shama said the meeting had not been cancelled but deferred until a mutually convenient time.
She described reports of its cancellation as misinformation, saying both sides had agreed that it would be better to hold the talks later when they were available.
The state minister also indicated that Bangladesh would host several high-level foreign visits in the coming days, although she did not disclose any names or tentative dates.
Asked whether water-sharing issues, particularly the Ganges water issue, had been discussed at a meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Shama said the government could hold extensive discussions with the prime minister on a range of issues.
However, she did not directly confirm whether the Ganges water issue had been discussed at the meeting.

item.title: Law and order returns to normal in Gopalganj amid intensified joint patrols
item.description:
The law and order situation in Gopalganj has returned to normal following a period of violence and unrest.
With Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel deployed and joint forces intensifying patrols, government and private offices, courts and shops across the district reopened on Monday morning. Traffic movement also returned to normal on the Dhaka-Khulna highway and roads within the district town.
Additional police and BGB personnel remain deployed at key locations across the town to prevent further incidents, while joint force patrols continue.
On Sunday, the district witnessed protests, arson and vandalism. Leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned, and its affiliated organisations have been accused of orchestrating the violence.
During the unrest, the homes of several BNP leaders were vandalised, and a Grameen Bank branch was set on fire. BGB personnel were subsequently deployed to bring the situation under control.
Meanwhile, amid the developments, the officers-in-charge (OCs) of three police stations in the district were transferred on Sunday night.
The officers are Ayub Ali of Tungipara Police Station, Riad Mahmud of Kotalipara Police Station and Mahfuzur Rahman of Kashiani Police Station. All three have been transferred to Kishoreganj district.

item.title: Govt plans to digitise all post offices by February 2028
item.description:
The government plans to transform all post offices across the country into digital service centres by February 2028 under two ongoing projects aimed at modernising postal services.
The initiatives will digitise the Postal Department’s financial services and introduce a national digital address database and route-mapping tool, the ‘Amar Dak’ app and the ‘Dak Bazar’ software.
Post, Telecommunications and Information Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam disclosed the plans on Monday while responding to a question from Rajshahi-5 MP Professor Nazrul Islam during the question-and-answer session on the sixth day of the fourth session of parliament.
The minister said a technical project titled “Sustainable and Modernisation of Mail Processing and Logistics Services” is being implemented from September 2024 to March 2027 to modernise postal operations and improve efficiency.
Another project, titled “Expansion and Accessibility of Existing Postal Services at Citizens’ Doorsteps”, is being implemented from March 2026 to February 2028.
Under the first project, the Postal Department’s existing electronic money transfer system is being upgraded to make it more modern and user-friendly.
The second project will digitise postal services through a national digital address database and route-mapping tool, the ‘Amar Dak’ app and the ‘Postal Rural Trade and Commerce Model’, known as ‘Dak Bazar’.
Once the projects are completed, all post offices will be transformed into digital service centres, allowing people across the country, including those in rural areas, to access secure digital postal services, the minister said.
Meanwhile, the minister outlined measures to prevent customer harassment, fraud and scams involving ‘Nagad’, the Postal Department’s digital financial service.
He said steps were being taken in line with directives from Bangladesh Bank, law enforcement agencies and the Directorate of Posts. Nagad provides round-the-clock customer support through its call centre at 16167, he said.
Currently, Nagad services are available at 97 post offices, while customer support is provided through a total of 113 service centres, including additional counters. Efforts are underway to gradually expand the network.
The minister said customers were regularly advised through awareness messages to keep their personal identification numbers (PINs) and one-time passwords (OTPs) confidential.
Suspicious transactions are also being monitored in coordination with relevant authorities to identify fraud networks.
Government allowances and other forms of assistance are now being transferred digitally and directly to beneficiaries’ accounts, he added.

item.title: Asean offers sidelined Myanmar leaders path back to talks
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Sunday to engage Myanmar’s government in stages, while making its return to high-level meetings conditional on progress on a regional peace plan.
Myanmar remains a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), but its political leaders have been barred from summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since October 2021.
The military seized power that year, overthrowing the elected government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi and triggering a civil war that continues today.
In a joint statement, the leaders called for “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.”
They said Asean could gradually restore Myanmar’s full political representation if it makes “sustained and concrete progress” on the bloc’s five-point peace plan. The plan has yielded little since it was agreed on in 2021, and fighting continues between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups.
“What more can we do for Myanmar?” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr asked at the leaders’ retreat in Manila. He urged the bloc to find practical ways to advance the peace plan and support an inclusive process led by Myanmar.
Thailand has pushed for closer engagement since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as civilian president this year following elections that monitors dismissed as a sham.
Leaders are also discussing trade, regional security and ways to share fuel supplies to cope with disruptions caused by the war in Iran. Australia and the Philippines signed a defense agreement on Sunday, while Canada and the Philippines announced on Saturday that they had concluded free trade negotiations.
A proposed code of conduct for the South China Sea remains unresolved. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said negotiations between Asean and China were 80% complete, but diplomats told AFP a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the summit.
US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive on Tuesday, toward the end of the summit, and meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other members of the Quad. The meeting is expected to precede talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.
Activists plan to march against Trump’s visit on Tuesday. Their protest is aimed in part at a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could displace Indigenous families.
The Philippines hands the rotating Asean chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due to take over in 2028.

item.title: COP31 faces deepening divides over climate finance, fossil fuel transition
item.description:
The final week of the UN climate summit COP31 opened on Monday with mounting pressure on governments to overcome divisions over climate finance, fossil fuel transition, adaptation and the rights of workers and vulnerable communities, as nearly 200 countries seek an agreement before the conference closes on November 20.
With more than 112 ministers expected to join high-level negotiations, the summit has entered a decisive phase. Australia is leading the negotiations while Türkiye holds the presidency, with both facing the challenge of translating existing climate commitments into measurable action.
At the heart of the negotiations is a widening divide between developed and developing countries over who should finance the global transition, how climate resources should be distributed and whether national energy pathways should be shaped by internationally agreed targets.
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has urged governments to avoid tactical delays and make progress on difficult issues.
The Australian-led negotiating process and Turkish presidency are working towards an overarching political declaration, known as the cover decision, intended to provide direction to the summit.
A proposed ministerial arrangement, called the Divan, will address five areas: adaptation, finance, mitigation, just transition and oceans.
However, negotiating blocs remain divided over the scope of the proposed declaration and its relationship with formal UN climate negotiations.
The Arab Group has opposed externally imposed sectoral targets and energy pathways that could undermine national priorities, while demanding that developed countries fulfil their financial commitments.
The African Group has stressed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, warning that electrification targets without adequate financial and technological support could place additional burdens on developing economies.
Least Developed Countries are demanding stronger adaptation measures, replenishment of climate funds and progress on implementing the first Global Stocktake, including support through the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.
One of Türkiye's major initiatives, the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from around 23% to 35% by 2035. More than 30 countries have backed the initiative.
The pledge promotes electrification across transport, buildings and industry, but its climate benefits will depend on the sources of electricity and investment in renewable energy, transmission networks and storage.
The target does not mean generating 35% of electricity from renewable sources. Without a parallel expansion of clean energy, growing electricity demand could also be met through fossil fuel generation.
The European Union wants COP31 to reinforce implementation of the first Global Stocktake and the transition away from fossil fuels.
However, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has cautioned against making an absolute clean-energy condition compulsory for participation in the electrification initiative.
China has also called for pragmatism and consensus while promoting renewable energy cooperation and investment.
Meanwhile, environmental and human rights organisations have warned that electrification without social and environmental safeguards could intensify pressure on communities affected by critical mineral extraction.
The debate has gained further significance as Türkiye promotes electrification while announcing new oil exploration activities.
Climate finance remains one of the most contentious issues at COP31, with developing countries demanding predictable, accessible and predominantly grant-based funding.
Under the COP29 agreement, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. The broader ambition is to scale up climate finance from all sources to at least $1.3 trillion annually by the same year.
However, a report presented by Brazil's COP30 presidency estimated that climate finance could reach only $458 billion-$461 billion annually by 2035 under a business-as-usual scenario, leaving a projected gap of approximately $840 billion against the $1.3 trillion ambition.
Stronger policy interventions could potentially increase annual finance flows to between $1.27 trillion and $1.41 trillion, according to the report.
Developing countries argue that private investment and loans cannot replace the financial obligations of developed countries under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement.
They also warn that loans on unfavourable terms could deepen debt burdens in economies already struggling with climate impacts and limited fiscal resources.
At a ministerial dialogue, Stiell highlighted the need to reduce the cost of capital, simplify access to finance and make funding more responsive to vulnerable economies.
The dispute over climate finance extends to adaptation and the growing costs of climate-related destruction.
The African Group is pushing for a tripling of adaptation finance, while civil society organisations have called for at least $120 billion annually well before 2035, with public grants playing a central role.
One negotiating proposal involves increasing adaptation finance from an estimated $40 billion baseline in 2025 to $120 billion by 2035. However, this remains under discussion rather than an agreed commitment.
The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage is also facing pressure to accelerate financial support.
Estimates by the Loss and Damage Collaboration put annual needs in developing countries at more than $724 billion. Meanwhile, requests amounting to approximately $2.8 billion have been made against an available funding envelope of around $342 million.
For countries such as Bangladesh, these financing gaps have immediate consequences. River erosion, flooding, salinity intrusion, displacement and infrastructure damage threaten livelihoods, public services and development gains.
The Just Transition Work Programme has emerged as another major negotiating challenge.
Countries broadly support a fair transition towards low-emission and climate-resilient economies but disagree over financing, governance and the establishment of a permanent Belém Action Mechanism under the UN climate process.
Civil society organisations and worker representatives want workers, women, young people, Indigenous Peoples, informal waste workers and affected communities to have meaningful roles in decision-making.
The debate extends beyond fossil fuel industries to agriculture, fisheries, transport and manufacturing, where changing energy systems and climate policies could reshape employment and livelihoods.
Gender negotiations have also exposed differences, although countries have adopted conclusions on the first year of the Belém Gender Action Plan for 2026–2034.
For Bangladesh, the negotiations carry significant implications for implementing its third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0).
Achieving national climate targets will require substantial investment, institutional coordination, technical capacity and international support.
A just transition must also protect farmers, fishers, industrial workers, women, young people and communities facing displacement.
Meaningful participation, predictable grant-based finance, skills development, stronger social protection and transparent accountability will be essential to ensure that climate commitments translate into tangible benefits.
Beyond formal negotiations, COP31's Action Agenda is highlighting investment initiatives in electricity grids, clean energy, zero-emission freight and methane reduction.
A memorandum involving British International Investment, Norway's Norfund and FinDev Canada under the 10by30 initiative aims to support at least $10 billion in climate investment activity over five years to 2030.
Six UN agencies have also launched a platform seeking to improve access to more than $3 billion in disaster risk financing by 2030, with the aim of protecting 75 million people and their livelihoods.
However, these announcements represent different types of investment commitments and initiatives, not necessarily new funding pledged at COP31 or money already disbursed.
For developing countries, the credibility of these initiatives will depend on whether announced investments become accessible finance and deliver measurable benefits to vulnerable communities.
The urgency of the negotiations is reinforced by the UN Environment Programme's Emissions Gap Report 2026, which projects approximately 2.8°C of global warming by 2100 under current policies.
Full implementation of existing national climate commitments would reduce the projection to around 2.6°C, still significantly above the Paris Agreement's temperature goals.
The report says the world has already lost the opportunity to avoid temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C threshold. The priority now is to minimise the scale and duration of the overshoot and establish a credible pathway back to 1.5°C.
Under the lowest-overshoot pathway assessed by UNEP, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to fall by 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
As COP31 approaches its November 20 conclusion, the international community faces a fundamental test: whether governments can move beyond political declarations and investment announcements to deliver the finance, technology and cooperation needed for climate action.
For developing countries, the outcome must address historical responsibility, financial inequality, adaptation needs and the protection of communities already experiencing the consequences of climate change.
Ultimately, COP31's success will be measured not by the number of pledges announced in Antalya, but by whether its decisions translate into real action for people and countries on the frontline of the climate crisis.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Death-row convict found hanging in Kashimpur prison
item.description:
A death-row convict in two murder cases was found hanging inside Kashimpur High-Security Central Prison in Gazipur early Monday.
The deceased, Farhad, 41, was the son of the late Hafiz Uddin of Shalinapara village in Tangail Sadar upazila.
Senior Jail Superintendent Mohammad Abdullah-Al-Mamun confirmed the incident, saying Farhad's body was discovered at around 1am in a ground-floor cell of the prison's Himel Building.
He said prison authorities had completed a routine headcount on Sunday before locking the cells for the night. Farhad, who had been sentenced to death for the murder of a man and a woman in Tangail, was sharing the cell with two co-accused.
During the night, the two inmates found him hanging from a cell window with a towel tied around his neck, the superintendent said.
Prison officials were alerted, recovered Farhad and rushed him to Gazipur Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead on arrival.
An inquest has been conducted, and the body will be handed over to the family after an autopsy, he added. Relatives have arrived at the prison.
The superintendent said Farhad was transferred to Kashimpur High-Security Prison from Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj on August 26, 2019.
He was being held in connection with two separate murder cases filed with Tangail police station, in which he had received death sentences.
Abdullah-Al-Mamun also said Farhad had been suffering from various health problems, including severe headaches and visual hallucinations, for around a year. He had received medical treatment at the prison hospital several times.

item.title: Chinmoy Krishna shifted from Chittagong jail to Keraniganj special prison
item.description:
Chinmoy Krishna Das Brahmachari, spokesperson for the Sanatani Jagaran Jote, has been transferred from Chittagong Central Jail to a special prison in Keraniganj, Dhaka.
He was transferred under tight security at around 5am on Monday (November 16), Chittagong Central Jail Senior Jail Superintendent Iqbal Hossain confirmed to Dhaka Tribune.
“Chinmoy Krishna Das has been taken to the special prison in Keraniganj, Dhaka,” he said, adding that he could not provide further details about the reasons for the sudden transfer.
Prison sources said Ranganath Das Brahmachari, who prepares meals for Chinmoy, was not transferred with him and remains at Chittagong Central Jail.
On October 31, 2024, Firoz Khan, then general secretary of the BNP's Mohra Ward unit in Chandgaon, filed a sedition case with Kotwali police against Chinmoy Krishna Das and 18 others over allegations of disrespecting the national flag.
Chinmoy was arrested in Dhaka on November 25, 2024, in connection with the case.
The following day, a Chittagong court rejected his bail petition and ordered him sent to jail. His supporters subsequently surrounded the prison van and staged protests on the court premises. Police fired sound grenades to disperse them before taking him to jail.
During the unrest, several motorcycles and vehicles were vandalised near the court. Later, lawyer Saiful Islam Alif was hacked and beaten to death near Rangam Convention Hall, allegedly by supporters of Chinmoy.
On November 29, 2024, Alif's father, Jamal Uddin, filed a murder case with Kotwali Police Station. The case statement named 31 people and accused another 15 to 16 unidentified individuals.
After completing the investigation, Assistant Commissioner of Chittagong Metropolitan Police (Kotwali) Mahfuzur Rahman submitted a charge sheet on July 1, 2025, naming 38 people as accused. Chinmoy Krishna Das was named as the prime accused.

America Invented the Drone War, So Why Is It Falling Behind?
item.description:
One mainstream document that called the United States’ sluggish reaction to this Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA) (and did so five years ago) was Christian Brose’s 2019 article in Foreign Affairs, “The New Revolution in Military Affairs: War’s Sci-Fi Future.” Brose’s bottom-line was the following: “Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, ubiquitous sensors, advanced manufacturing, and quantum science will transform warfare as radically as the technologies that consumed Bloch [a nineteenth-century founder of the concept of RMAs]. And yet the U.S. government’s thinking about how to employ these new technologies is not keeping pace with their development.”

Editorial note: This is the second in a four-part series from former National Geospatial-Intelligence Director VADM Frank Whitworth (Ret.) on the reluctant revolution in military affairs and what it means for future intelligence and defense. This series of perspectives was adapted from a previous white paper written by the author two years ago, while he was on active duty.

Brose correctly identified a history of “change labels” in the last three decades with no resulting or substantial adjustment to core military methods. This trend began with the oncoming “military technical revolution” in 1992, moved to Admiral Arthur Cebrowski’s “Network-Centric Warfare” in the mid-1990s, Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s “transformation” in the 9/11 era, and Deputy Secretary Robert Work’s “third offset strategy” in 2014. Each brought a slight twist on a common theme: “…emerging technologies will enable new battle networks of sensors and shooters to rapidly accelerate the process of detecting, targeting, and striking threats.”

Brose did not stop there. He was critical of American procurement choices over the last three decades as Washington “…poured money into newer versions of old military platforms and prayed for technological miracles to come (which often became acquisition debacles when those miracles did not materialize.” Brose was prescient in identifying how inexpensive uncrewing could be – and how much change it required of the military mindset. Well before Replicator (DOD’s primary development program for autonomous vehicles) became a glimmer in anyone’s eye, Brose identified the need for fleets of drones, with ubiquitous communications and elements of autonomy.

To reiterate, this paper does not intend to prove and explain the United States’ reluctant acceptance of every facet of this “drones, codes, and spacecraft” RMA. In fact, during our application of Marshall’s principles, we cited three major developments that help rule-out our reluctance to accept non-proximate warfare in the space and cyber domains: specifically, the establishment of the United States Space Force, USPACECOM, and USCYBERCOM. Drones are a different matter, though – and to prove our reluctance, we will (a) compare the United States’ rate of “military drone fleet” development to that of Ukraine, and (b) demonstrate the stark difference in DOD’s acquisition budgets between manned and unmanned assets.

Globally, the number of nations with armed drone programs has accelerated. The rapid growth of armed, medium altitude, long endurance (MALE) drones (such as the MQ-9 Reaper) since 2001 is evident in this graphic from Drone Wars UK:

Source: Drone Wars UK

These large, MALE drones are important because they can deliver munitions lengthy distances and damage strategic targets such as infrastructure and headquarters. Since Russia’s invasion in 2022, Ukraine has transformed itself into a world leader of drone technology and employment. In fact, Ukrainian President Zelensky just announced in December 2024 that his country will produce 30,000 MALE drones next year. That nearly triples DOD’s entire drone fleet of 11,000 (a number that even includes smaller, non-MALE assets such as the hand-launched RQ-11B Raven). The United States’ production of military drones has been lapped numerically by Ukraine in only two years—despite America’s 20-year head-start in developing the technology.

The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense Transformation reports seven drone models were produced domestically in 2022, and that number has grown tenfold to 67 in only two years. Similarly, Ukraine now has an astounding 200 domestic drone manufacturers. This stands in stark contrast to America’s drone manufacturing sector, which has declined. With the United States’ withdrawal from Afghanistan and a reduction in military contracts, IBIS World estimates the United States has only 73 businesses in the UAV manufacturing sector. As representationally depicted in Figure 3, the sector is declining at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 5.8 percent to $4.0 billion through 2024 (dropping 21.4 percent this year alone.)

UAV Manufacturing in the U.S. — Source: IBISWorld

In examining expenditures reported in the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense, Comptroller’s April 4, 2024 report, “Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System, FY2025,” the United States’ reluctance to adopting the “drones” portion of this RMA is demonstrated further. As depicted in Figure 4, unmanned aircraft systems account for less than four percent of DOD’s expenditures dedicated to overall aviation and related systems. Separately, there are no “unmanned” wedges in either the $48 billion of proposed expenditures for shipbuilding and maritime systems or the $13 billion or proposed expenditures for ground systems. To be fair to the Navy, they do lead the other services in Research and Development for unmanned systems – but those investments will require time before they are made manifest in the fleet.

Figure 4: DOD’s FY2025 Aviation Expenditures — Source: DOD Comptroller

item.title: The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve
item.description:
The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve Expert comment jon.wallace 17 November 2026

This week’s summit did not produce the Code many desire. But as ASEAN Chair Manila has laid a useful foundation for the Code, while making important progress on regional connectivity.

When it assumed the Chair of ASEAN last year, the Philippines placed negotiations to establish a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) at the centre of its agenda. An agreement has been desired for decades, to help reduce territorial and other tensions between China and regional countries. The need for the COC is clear: Philippine ships have continued to clash with Chinese Coast Guard vessels throughout the year, around disputed areas such as Scarborough Shoal. 

But Philippines Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cooled expectations of an agreement at this week’s ASEAN summit. In a recent statement, she said that while around 80 per cent of the provisions are agreed, ‘sticking points’ still remain. It is therefore unlikely to be concluded by the end of the year with Philippines as ASEAN Chair.

But the Philippines tenure has been about more than just the COC. In a region of diverging priorities, security alignments, and threat perceptions, Manila should be judged by how far it has boosted ASEAN’s utility as an independent diplomatic actor able to strengthen regional solidarity.

Progress under pressure

The role of ASEAN Chair was clearly going to test the Philippines: How would it reconcile its national security interests with its responsibilities as the leader of a forum for regional cooperation? And would Beijing see Manila as a good faith actor on the COC?

The Philippines is, after all, one of the oldest treaty partners of the US. Those ties are getting stronger under President Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos, while its relationship with China becomes ever more fractious – a stance not shared by all ASEAN partners. 

Beside these obvious impediments, the overlapping and complex nature of the claims in South China Sea waters made the COC a tricky subject to negotiate within the bloc, let alone with China. But under the stewardship of the Philippines delegations met every month this year and have managed to produce a substantial part of an agreement – a significant jump after two decades of diplomatic deadlock. 

There is no official confirmation on what the sticking points were, but past statements suggest issues around legal implementation, geographical scope, and terms of reference prevented a final agreement. Singapore, next year’s chair, enjoys a more stable relationship with Beijing and may stand a better chance of ironing out these final elements. Even this remains uncertain, but setting up Singapore with the best possible chance always looked like the most realistic ambition for the Philippines on the COC, and it has made good progress to that end. 

Outside of COC negotiations, the Philippines has managed to make significant moves on some other stated priorities. The Philippines assumed the Chair of ASEAN under the theme ‘Navigating our future, together’. This focussed on three core pillars: Peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment. 

To this end, Manila concluded negotiations of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). This is the world’s first binding region-wide digital economy deal, which will better integrate the region and foster greater cross-border data flows and end-to-end digital trade, promising to bring in $2 trillion by 2030. 

The Philippines also championed the ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration on Strategic Trade Management, which aims to establish unified frameworks to strengthen the resilience of regional supply chains. 

And it established the ASEAN Centre of Excellence for Creative Industries, fostering a more interconnected creative economy and greater cultural exchange. Manila has also pushed for greater collaboration on disaster preparedness, with a focus on pooling resources in the face of natural calamities.

One significant area where little has been achieved is the crisis in Myanmar: diplomatic progress on the issue was a strategic and symbolic challenge for the Philippines and ASEAN’s credibility as a peace-making body. In the end, ASEAN’s agenda remains stalled. The summit agreed to pursue ‘calibrated engagement’ in pursuit of ASEAN’s ‘5 Point Consensus’, and leaves the door open for gradual restoration to the bloc. But as a unified group, ASEAN appears to have little hope of influencing Myanmar’s military government.

Successful summitry 

This summit needed to go well for President Marcos. The Philippines has been pursuing its ASEAN agenda at a time of mounting domestic pressure. The war in Iran has strained energy supply chains, hindering access to necessities. Summer saw massive losses from tsunamis and earthquakes, and impeachment proceedings against the Vice President. The Marcos administration received its lowest ever approval ratings this month, as protestors clashed with police on the eve of the summit.

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

The event was ostensibly been productive. More than 150 outcome documents were reviewed and approved. A new ASEAN free trade agreement has been agreed with Canada. Brazil and Canada have committed $540 million for rainforest protection. And the event presented a significant opportunity for the bloc to interact with influential leaders including President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Prime Minister Mark Carney, and President Lula da Silva.

And as always at summits, meetings on the sidelines provided opportunities for important diplomacy: Japan’s PM Takaichi and South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung held their fourth bilateral meeting. And the Quad convened for the first time in two years. 

But ASEAN countries must see real returns from these convenings to be considered a success. And it is imperative that ASEAN as a unit is seen as a key player rather than a platform through which bilateral deals can be done. Indeed, Philippines President Marcos emphasized a ‘whole-of-ASEAN approach’ in his plenary speech.

This focus on unifying regional interests is not for the sake of ASEAN alone, but part of a wider strategy to protect the Philippines in the face of broader geopolitical trends. The test will be if Manila can carry this sentiment forward beyond its tenure as chair – something that may prove difficult.

Preparing for the storms ahead

2027 will see Singapore become ASEAN Chair with the organization set to be tested by deepening faultlines on AI alliances, critical mineral exploration, and supply chain and energy resilience. 

Divergences are already appearing among members on how best to approach these issues. Coming on top of existing territorial disputes, strained relations within the bloc seem likely. However, even if ASEAN countries have diverging interests, they will never be able to escape the reality of what they share: geography and history. 

As the overlapping threats of climate change, great power rivalry, and an unstable global economy demand a cohesive regional response, the Philippines’ priorities of cohesion and greater interdependence will be key to the region’s survival. What this year has made clear is that grand international dealmaking of the kind represented by the COC may continue to prove difficult for the group. Despite this, ASEAN can provide an indispensable function, facilitating interoperability and integration that fuels growth and secures sovereignty. 

As President Marcos said at the summit’s opening, the coming years will be about ‘not only where ASEAN is headed, but what ASEAN must become’. For years the ASEAN has been dismissed as ineffectual and underperforming. But the group has endured. And the Philippines period as Chair has perhaps shown the bloc’s true value – driving incremental but unyielding change towards an increasingly interconnected region.

item.description:
JERUSALEM, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to select a new speaker opposed to the agenda of Benjamin Netanyahu, a potential first step in rolling back theprime minister's divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.

Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the parliament.

item.title: Israel parliament elects Eisenkot ally as speaker in blow for Netanyahu
item.description:
Israeli lawmakers on Tuesday elected a parliament speaker from the camp opposed to caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a first step towards rolling back the legacy of the country's divisive veteran leader.

Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.

Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.
